orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, carrying straight on from the end of Chapter XV: it is the same Sunday night, in March 1784. Partway through, Lockwood steps in for a sentence or two when Nelly asks him a question, and then she goes on.

notes.t: the Catherine you saw at Wuthering Heights
notes.g: The young Mrs. Heathcliff whom Lockwood met in Chapters II and III.
notes.n: So the second Catherine is born here, the daughter of Catherine and Edgar Linton, as Nelly hinted in Chapter IV.

notes.g: A tiny, weak baby, born two months early.
notes.n: Premature babies rarely survived then. 'Puny' means small and sickly.

notes.m: 'Distraction' here means near-madness from sorrow, not a loss of focus. 'The latter' is the second-named person, Edgar.

notes.g: The loss of someone close through death.

notes.t: its after-effects showed how deep the sorrow sunk
notes.g: What it did to him later showed how deep his grief went.

notes.t: his being left without an heir
notes.g: Edgar had no son to inherit his estate.
notes.n: A daughter did not count as an 'heir' under the arrangement Nelly describes next.
'Orphan' could mean a child who had lost just one parent.

notes.g: I silently cursed old Mr. Linton.
notes.m: 'Abuse' here means to insult or scold, in words.

notes.g: Edgar and Isabella's late father, old Mr. Linton.
notes.n: He and his wife died in Chapter IX.

notes.t: the securing his estate to his own daughter, instead of his son’s
notes.g: Old Mr. Linton's will left the Grange, if Edgar had no son, to his own daughter Isabella rather than to Edgar's daughter.
notes.n: Arrangements like this ('settling' an estate) were common, to keep land in the family line. Isabella is now Heathcliff's wife, and a wife's property was her husband's (see Chapters X and XIII).

notes.g: A baby nobody greeted with joy.
We made up for the neglect later.

notes.t: as friendless as its end is likely to be
notes.g: As lonely as Nelly fears the rest of her life will be.
notes.n: Nelly is speaking in 1801, when young Catherine is a widow living unhappily at the Heights (Chapters II and IV).
Blinds and curtains were closed in a house where someone had died.

notes.g: The bed and the person lying on it.
notes.n: 'Couch' here means a bed, not a sofa.

notes.g: The stillness of someone worn out by grief.
In a more devout state of mind.
notes.n: 'Frame of mind' was often shortened to 'frame'.

notes.g: The rest God gives the dead.
notes.n: Christian language: the righteous dead 'rest in peace' with God.

notes.t: Incomparably beyond and above us all!
notes.g: Nelly repeats Catherine's own words from Chapter XV.
notes.n: There Catherine said she would soon be 'incomparably beyond and above you all'.

notes.t: her spirit is at home with God
notes.n: A phrase echoing St. Paul: to be 'absent from the body' is to be 'present with the Lord' (2 Corinthians 5:8).

notes.t: watching in the chamber of death
notes.g: Sitting up with a dead body in its room.
notes.n: Families kept watch beside the dead, day and night, until the funeral.

notes.g: A wildly grieving or hopeless mourner.
The endless, bright life after death.
Catherine's death, seen as a happy escape from suffering.
Deserved a safe, peaceful resting place.

notes.t: a pledge of equal quiet to its former inhabitant
notes.g: A promise that her soul, which lived in the body, was at peace too.

notes.t: Do you believe such people are happy in the other world, sir?
notes.g: Nelly asks Lockwood whether someone like Catherine can be happy after death.
notes.n: Her story pauses here and we are briefly back in 1801, by Lockwood's bed.
Lockwood thinks it a slightly improper question. Church teaching said the wicked were damned; Nelly is wondering aloud whether that applies to Catherine.

notes.t: Retracing the course of Catherine Linton
the gallop of the messenger going to Gimmerton
notes.g: The sound of a rider sent galloping to the village, probably for the doctor.
The private grounds around the Grange.
notes.m: Not a public park: the enclosed land of a country house.

notes.g: A tall tree common in English woods and hedges.

notes.n: 'Ouzel' is an old name for the blackbird. The birds ignore Heathcliff as if he were a tree.

notes.g: Don't whimper in front of me.

notes.t: he had got intelligence of the catastrophe
notes.g: He had already learned of the disaster.
His heart was subdued; he had calmed down.

notes.n: Preachers urged people to take warning from death and turn from sin before it was too late.

notes.t: a true history of the event
notes.g: An accurate account of what happened.

notes.n: Here: he was forced to lean on something for support.

notes.g: Your pride can't hide your feelings from God.
As quietly as a lamb: peacefully, without struggle.

notes.m: 'Latest' here means last, final, not 'most recent so far'.

notes.g: Heathcliff turns Nelly's blessing into a curse.
notes.n: Nelly had said 'may she wake as kindly in the other world'.

notes.t: Catherine Earnshaw, may you not rest as long as I am living
notes.g: Heathcliff prays that Catherine's spirit will not rest in peace while he lives.
notes.n: He calls her by her maiden name. Think back to Lockwood's night in Chapter III, and Heathcliff at the window.

notes.t: The murdered do haunt their murderers
notes.g: An old folk belief that murder victims haunt their killers.
notes.n: Catherine accused him of killing her in Chapter XV, so he takes her at her word.
A 'goad' is a pointed stick for driving cattle.

notes.g: The coffin lid stayed off, so people could see her.
notes.n: The dead were laid out at home before the funeral, for family and friends to pay their respects.
Originally the 'withdrawing room', where the family withdrew after a meal.
'Adieu' is French for goodbye, literally 'to God'.

notes.t: a curl of light hair, fastened with a silver thread
notes.g: A lock of Edgar's fair hair, tied with silver thread.
notes.n: Edgar is fair-haired; Heathcliff is dark.

notes.g: A small hinged case worn on a chain, holding a keepsake.
notes.n: Lovers and family often kept a lock of each other's hair in one.

notes.t: a black lock of his own
notes.g: A strand of his own black hair.

notes.t: I twisted the two, and enclosed them together
notes.g: Nelly twisted both locks of hair together and put them in the locket.
notes.n: So Catherine is buried with both men's hair.

notes.t: attend the remains of his sister to the grave
notes.g: Follow his sister's body to her burial.
He sent no apology for staying away.
Farmers who rented land from Edgar.

notes.n: Edgar cut off contact with her after she married Heathcliff (Chapter XIV).

notes.t: under the carved monument of the Lintons
notes.g: Inside the church, under the Linton family memorial.
notes.n: Gentry families were often buried inside the church. In Chapter XII Catherine said she wanted to lie 'not among the Lintons, mind, under the chapel-roof, but in the open air'.

notes.t: the tombs of her own relations, outside
notes.g: The Earnshaw graves out in the churchyard.

notes.n: 'Kirk' is the northern and Scottish word for church.

notes.g: Heather and low moorland shrubs bearing small dark berries.
notes.n: Bilberries are a wild cousin of the blueberry.

notes.g: Crumbly black peat soil from the moor.

notes.t: Her husband lies in the same spot now
notes.g: Edgar is now buried beside her.
notes.n: Nelly is telling the story in 1801, when Edgar is dead: she called him 'my late master' in Chapter IV.

notes.t: a plain grey block at their feet
notes.g: A plain footstone marking the end of each grave.
